source: The five-input opening's declared assumptions, in one file so the room and engines/opening.js never inline a figure. The withdrawal rate is 3.5% because this audience faces fifty- to sixty-year retirements: the 4% convention was fitted to thirty-year windows (Bengen 1994, the Trinity study), and the early-retirement literature (Early Retirement Now's safe withdrawal series; the Trinity update for longer horizons) puts a sixty-year horizon nearer 3.25% to 3.5%. The three real returns bracket data/return_bands.json's planning bands from below: 3%, 5% and 7% real, so the band is honest about a stock-heavy portfolio without promising the all-equity long-run average.
confidenceNote: Planning conventions, not findings. Every figure here is shown in the opening's assumptions drawer with this note and can be changed there for the session; nothing here is a fact about a household.
note: Read by engines/opening.js. withdrawalPoints are the Triple D points the drawer shows beside the 3.5% default: the 4% convention and the 3.25% floor. realReturns are the three runs behind the FI date band: worst plausible, likely, best plausible. stages are the Advice Translator's early lines: below `investedBelowYears` years of spending invested, the stage applies; the last stage has no ceiling. leverIds name the levers in data/levers.json the opening ranks, in the order ties break. Money in cents.
unknownSpendingNote: When someone does not know what they spend, seven tenths of take-home stands in, tagged rough: the median household saves in the teens of take-home, so seven tenths overstates spending a little and understates the date, which is the safer error on an opening screen.
raiseRateNote: The real raise rate the save-half-of-every-raise lever assumes: 2% a year over inflation, a career's typical early-years pace rather than a whole-career average.
debtPayoffNote: A debt with no minimum payment entered is priced as a five-year level payment at its rate, so 'clear the dearest debt' can say what it frees. A stated stand-in, never a fact.

stages.line: Right now income and savings rate are almost all of your outcome. Returns barely matter yet.
Your portfolio now does real work. Fees, allocation, and which account you use start to matter.
